name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: The first egg box
items.fact: The egg box was invented in 1911 by Joseph Coyle, a newspaper editor in British Columbia, Canada, to end an argument between a farmer and a hotel about broken eggs.

items.name: Bubble wrap
items.fact: Bubble wrap was invented in 1957 by two engineers in New Jersey who were trying to make a textured wallpaper. It failed as wallpaper, but became famous for protecting computers.

items.name: Square chocolate
items.fact: Ritter Sport chocolate is square because, in 1932, Clara Ritter wanted a bar that would fit into a sports jacket pocket without breaking.

items.name: Wine in a box
items.fact: Boxed wine was invented in Australia in 1965 by the winemaker Thomas Angove. With the first version, customers cut the corner off the bag and closed it again with a peg.

items.name: The pizza saver
items.fact: The little plastic “table” in the middle of a pizza box, which stops the lid sticking to the cheese, was patented in 1985 by Carmela Vitale from New York State.

items.name: Edible six-pack rings
items.fact: A small brewery in Florida made six-pack rings from barley and wheat left over from brewing, so that if they ended up in the sea, animals could eat them safely.

items.name: The flat-bottomed paper bag
items.fact: The flat-bottomed paper bag came from a machine invented by Margaret Knight around 1870. A man copied her idea and claimed it as his own, but she won in court.

items.name: The bent-neck toilet cleaner
items.fact: The bent neck of the Toilet Duck bottle was invented in Switzerland in 1980, so that people could squirt cleaner under the rim of the toilet without bending down.

items.name: The 57 on a ketchup bottle
items.fact: The “57” on the neck of a glass Heinz ketchup bottle marks the best place to tap. Heinz says a firm tap there gets the ketchup flowing.

items.name: Salt in a paper twist
items.fact: Early British crisps came unsalted, with a small twist of blue paper full of salt inside the bag, so that people could add as much salt as they wanted.

fakes.name: The fondue pot pack
fakes.fact: A Swiss cheese maker sold ready-made fondue in a paper pack shaped like a small pot that could go straight on the cooker. It was dropped when the handles caught fire.

fakes.name: The spaghetti ruler
fakes.fact: An Italian pasta maker sold spaghetti in tall paper tubes with a ruler printed on the side, so you could measure one portion by its height.

fakes.name: Butter paper that changes colour
fakes.fact: A Danish dairy wraps its butter in paper that changes from white to pale yellow when the butter is soft enough to spread.

fakes.name: The thumb-shaped dent
fakes.fact: A Belgian brewery gives its bottles a dent on one side, copied from the brewer's own thumb, so that the bottle doesn't slip out of wet hands.

fakes.name: The clog-shaped sweet box
fakes.fact: A Dutch liquorice company sold its sweets in a box shaped like a wooden clog. It stopped after shops complained that the boxes kept falling over.

fakes.name: The dated wax seal
fakes.fact: A Polish jam maker seals each jar with a layer of wax stamped with the date the fruit was picked, not the date the jam was made.

fakes.name: The whistling coffee bag
fakes.fact: A Finnish coffee brand added a valve to its bags that whistles softly when you squeeze the bag, but only while the beans inside are still fresh.

fakes.name: The mountain chocolate bar
fakes.fact: An Austrian chocolate bar is shaped like a mountain range: each piece you break off is the shape of a real Alpine peak, with its height printed underneath.

fakes.name: The weather-forecast milk carton
fakes.fact: A Norwegian dairy printed the next week's weather forecast on its milk cartons, because farmers said they read the carton at breakfast more often than the newspaper.

fakes.name: The bread-bag clock
fakes.fact: A Swiss bakery printed a small clock face on its paper bread bags, with the hand pointing to the hour when that loaf came out of the oven.
